In Indian sporting history, few careers carry an irony as striking as that of MJ Gopalan. A gifted cricketer and hockey player, Gopalan found himself facing an extraordinary choice in 1936: pursue a place in the Indian hockey team for the Berlin Olympics under legendary captain Dhyan Chand, or travel to England with the Indian cricket side. He chose cricket, following his greater passion. But what followed made the decision one of the most fascinating "what if" moments in Indian sport. The Indian hockey team went on to win Olympic gold in Berlin, while Gopalan, despite being part of the cricket tour he had chosen, did not get an opportunity to play a Test in England. Gopalan was a genuine double international, representing India in both cricket and hockey. Born in Morappakam and raised in Triplicane, Chennai, he emerged as a fast-medium bowler capable of moving the ball both ways and became one of the leading figures in Madras cricket. His cricketing talent was spotted by CP Johnstone, one of the founding figures of Madras cricket, and Gopalan soon made his mark in local cricket. His first-class career eventually brought him 194 wickets and 2,916 runs in 78 matches, making him far more successful at that level than his modest international record would suggest.

Cricket over Berlin Olympics with Dhyan Chand

Gopalan's hockey career was also significant. He played as a centre-half and, in 1935, toured New Zealand with the Indian hockey side, which enjoyed considerable success. That experience put him firmly in the reckoning for the 1936 Olympic squad. But when the opportunity came to compete for a place in the hockey team for the Berlin Games, Gopalan chose not to pursue the Olympic route. Instead, he accepted his place on the cricket tour of England. It was a decision that looked very different once the Berlin Olympics were over. India, led by Dhyan Chand, produced one of the most dominant campaigns in Olympic hockey history and won the gold medal after defeating Germany 8-1 in the final. Gopalan, who had been faced with the possibility of being part of that historic side, was instead in England with the cricket team. The irony became even greater because his opportunities on the cricket tour were limited. With Mohammad Nissar and Amar Singh ahead of him, Gopalan was not expected to play a major role, and he ultimately did not play a Test in England.

Gopalan had already made his Test debut before the 1936 tour, playing his only Test for India against England at Calcutta in the 1933-34 season. He took one wicket and scored 18 runs. Despite his reputation in domestic cricket, that remained his only appearance at Test level. His first-class record, however, reflected the quality of the cricketer he was. Gopalan took 194 wickets and scored 2,916 runs in 78 matches, while his batting improved significantly as his career progressed. He also captained Madras for several years and remained one of the most influential figures in the city's cricketing circles for around 25 years. But perhaps the most remarkable chapter of Gopalan's cricket career came not in Test cricket, but at the very beginning of India's premier domestic competition.

He bowled the first ball in Ranji Trophy history

When the Ranji Trophy was inaugurated in 1934, Madras and Mysore played the competition's first-ever match. Gopalan was given the honour of bowling the first delivery in Ranji Trophy history. That moment ensured that, regardless of the brevity of his Test career, his name would remain permanently linked to one of the most important competitions in Indian cricket. The Ranji Trophy would become the country's premier first-class tournament and a crucial pathway for generations of Indian cricketers. Gopalan's legacy in Madras cricket continued well beyond his playing career. He later served as a national selector in the 1950s and remained a respected figure in Indian cricket. In 1952, a silver jubilee fund was started to mark his 25 years in cricket and hockey, while the annual contest between Madras and Ceylon was named the MJ Gopalan Trophy. The competition continued for decades, underlining the esteem in which he was held.

Gopalan's connection with Chennai cricket was eventually honoured at the city's iconic MA Chidambaram Stadium. One of the entrances at the famous Chepauk stadium is named after him, ensuring that his name remains part of the physical landscape of Indian cricket. His career therefore presents a remarkable contradiction. He was good enough to represent India in two sports and was considered for an Olympic hockey team captained by Dhyan Chand, yet his cricket career at the highest international level consisted of only one Test. The England tour that he chose over the Berlin Olympics did not give him the opportunities he might have expected, while the hockey team he left behind returned from Germany as Olympic champions. Yet Gopalan's choice should not simply be viewed as a mistake. Cricket was his passion, and in 1936 he chose the sport he loved. What makes the decision so compelling is the benefit of hindsight. Had he pursued hockey and made the Olympic squad, he could have been part of Dhyan Chand's gold-medal-winning team and one of the most celebrated sporting groups in India's history. Instead, he became part of a different kind of history. He chose cricket over a chance at Olympic gold with Dhyan Chand, played only one Test for India, but bowled the first ball in Ranji Trophy history. His name lives on at Chepauk, his first-class record remains impressive, and his story continues to stand as one of Indian sport's great unanswered "what ifs". Gopalan died in December 2003 after a long life in Indian sport. At the time of his death, he was regarded as the oldest surviving Test cricketer.

articles.title: ‘I urge other cricketers to speak up’: Moin Khan makes emotional appeal for Imran Khan
articles.summary: Cricket News: NEW DELHI: Former Pakistan wicketkeeper-batter Moin Khan has joined the growing chorus of voices expressing concern over the deteriorating health of f.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former Pakistan wicketkeeper-batter Moin Khan has joined the growing chorus of voices expressing concern over the deteriorating health of former Pakistan captain and 1992 World Cup-winning leader Imran Khan, urging the country's authorities to ensure that the 73-year-old receives proper medical treatment in jail.Moin, a key member of Pakistan's World Cup-winning side under Imran, released an emotional video message on Saturday in which he appealed to the government, Adiala jail authorities and fellow cricketers to stand up for the former all-rounder. His intervention came shortly after batting great Javed Miandad also made an impassioned appeal in support of Imran.Imran has been incarcerated at Adiala jail in Rawalpindi since 2023 after being convicted in corruption cases, which he continues to deny. Concerns over his health have intensified in recent months, with reports of medical problems and allegations of inadequate medical care.‘His right to medical care should be honoured’Moin, who played alongside Imran during Pakistan's celebrated 1992 World Cup campaign, said the former captain's contribution to Pakistan cricket could not be forgotten and urged authorities to fulfil his right to receive medical treatment.“Our captain Imran Khan, as you all know, is currently in Adiala jail, and his condition is quite bad at present. One more time, I will urge the authorities, the government of Pakistan and all those people who run the Adiala jail,” Moin said in his video.“My request is that our captain’s right, as a former prime minister, as a citizen of Pakistan, his right to medical care should be honoured. Whatever he needs, it should be seen to,” he added.Moin then made a direct appeal to fellow cricketers to publicly support Imran.“Besides, I also urge other cricketers to speak up and voice their support for him. Imran Khan’s contribution to Pakistan cricket [is immense] and all of us who played in his era learnt a lot from him. He has given Pakistan cricket a lot,” he said.The plea comes amid increasing concern over Imran's health and follows a similar public appeal from Miandad. Pakistan's Supreme Court recently ordered that Imran be taken to hospital for medical examinations. He was subsequently taken to hospital before being returned to prison.Former cricketers rally behind ImranThe concerns have also prompted a group of former international captains to call for better medical care for Imran. 22 former captains from countries including India, England, the West Indies and New Zealand wrote to Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif seeking adequate healthcare and constitutional safeguards for the former Pakistan captain. The letter followed an earlier appeal by 14 former captains in February.Australia captain Pat Cummins has also publicly backed the former captains' appeal.Australia great Greg Chappell, who played an important role in bringing former cricketers together in support of Imran, recently painted a worrying picture of his condition.“At the moment, he's not getting any better. You know, from a physical point of view, it's hard to get information, but I saw a video clip the other day, I'm assuming, of his latest trip to hospital where he was put into a wheelchair to get him to, from wherever he was, to wherever he was going, and he didn't look well at all. He didn't look robust. He didn't look like he could really... get around very much,” Chappell said.“I mean, 73 years of age, so obviously, you know, he's getting older, but, you know, I met up with him in Pakistan 6 years ago, and he was still a strong, robust older man. That's not the case anymore. His right eye apparently [has developed a disability]… he's struggling. He's been in isolation for 3 years,” he added.The issue has also spilled into the cricketing world. The Pakistan Cricket Board lodged a formal complaint against Sky Sports after an interview with Imran's sons, Suleiman and Kasim Khan, was aired during the lunch break on the first day of the ongoing Test at Lord's.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Off-field stuff, we don’t focus on it': Muzumdar refuses to be drawn into India-Pakistan handshake debate
articles.summary: Cricket News: India women's head coach Amol Muzumdar on Saturday refused to be drawn into questions over the handshake protocol ahead of the team's Women's Asia Cup.
articles.body: India women's head coach Amol Muzumdar on Saturday refused to be drawn into questions over the handshake protocol ahead of the team's Women's Asia Cup clash against Pakistan on September 5.With India set to face Pakistan again, Muzumdar said the team was focused solely on its opening game against Thailand on Sunday and would address the issue when the two sides meet.“We try to play the best cricket on the ground and off the field stuff, we don't focus on it. We try to play the best cricket that we know on that particular day. We will speak about this when we play that game. But at the moment, we are focusing on tomorrow's game. One game at a time,” Muzumdar said at the pre-match press conference.Handshake protocol continuesThe no-handshake stance between Indian and Pakistani cricket teams has been in place since the 2025 Men's Asia Cup, following the Pahalgam terror attack in April that year. India avoided handshakes with Pakistan in all three meetings during that tournament, including the final. The stance was subsequently maintained across senior, women's and age-group cricket.The Indian women's team followed the protocol during their Women's ODI World Cup meeting with Pakistan in Colombo in October 2025. It was also observed during the Men's Rising Stars Asia Cup, the Under-19 Asia Cup, the Under-19 World Cup and the Men's T20 World Cup.The stance continued during the Women's T20 World Cup clash between India and Pakistan in Birmingham in June 2026, when Harmanpreet Kaur's team again did not exchange handshakes with their opponents.India look to move on from poor T20I formMuzumdar also played down India's recent T20I record, with the team having lost nine of their 16 matches this year. The coach acknowledged that there is plenty of room for improvement but backed the young side to develop its aggressive style of cricket.“We don't pay too much attention to the form. You are talking about 16 T20Is in the last six months. But at the same time, we know what scope of improvement this team has got,” he said.“There is a huge scope of improvement. There is a young side. We are trying to play some good cricket, good aggressive cricket,'' he added.India will begin their Women's T20 Asia Cup campaign against Thailand on Sunday before turning their attention to the much-anticipated Pakistan clash on September 5.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: County Championship: Durham need four runs to beat Gloucestershire
articles.summary: Division Two leaders Durham will need four runs on the final day to beat Gloucestershire.
articles.body:
Rothesay County Championship, Division Two, Chester-le-Street (day three)

Gloucestershire 137: Aldridge 5-16 & 250: Hammond 58; Aldridge 4-47

Durham 384: Bedingham 122; Langridge 3-89

Durham (6 pts) need four runs to beat Gloucs (3 pts)

Bad light prevented Kasey Aldridge's superb nine-wicket match haul from delivering league leaders Durham a three-day County Championship win over bottom side Gloucestershire.

A devastating burst of 4-47 from the seam-bowling all-rounder backed up his first innings five-for, but the hosts' victory charge will roll into day four with only four to win as the weather meant their chase could not begin before close.

At the start of the day, Durham's tail boosted their first-innings total to 384 - a lead of 247 - thanks to cameos from Aldridge, Brydon Carse and Matthew Potts, before the latter pair reduced Gloucestershire to 7-2 second time around. They were later bowled out for 250.

Cameron Bancroft and Miles Hammond were able to guide the visitors to 50-2 at lunch.

A century stand for the fourth wicket halted Durham's progress before Aldridge produced a superb three-wicket spell on the brink of tea to reaffirm the home side's dominance in the match and the Division Two table.

Light dictated that Durham's Test-quality pace attack step aside with two wickets required, and an explosive 10th-wicket partnership of 39 between Sai Kishore (29 not out) and JT Langridge forced the league leaders to bat again.

With that target of four set, the players did not emerge from their dressing rooms, with Gloucestershire refusing to bowl spin, leaving as little as one ball of action in prospect for day four.

In the only fixture in the country to start on time, Durham resumed on 331-8 and swiftly accelerated beyond 350.

Carse took James Hayes for 16 in an over before he was bowled by the Nottinghamshire loanee for 20. Potts, who added 15, fell to Langridge, the seamer finishing with three wickets.

The England duo then produced a relentless opening burst which saw Gloucestershire stagger to 15-2 in 10 overs.

Joe Phillips was removed by Carse for the second time in the match for a duck, before Potts had Ollie Price caught behind. Bancroft and Hammond counter-attacked against the change bowlers to reach lunch with no further damage.

Both sides battled manfully after the break, with the left-handed Hammond negotiating a testing nine-over Ben Stokes spell to reach 50 off 80 balls.

He batted comfortably in partnership with captain Bancroft, but a rising delivery from Aldridge squared Hammond up and induced the edge for 58.

Aldridge continued his fine performance by having Bancroft caught at second slip for 46 in his next over, and new man Tommy Boorman followed shortly after.

Gloucestershire finished the session five down and still 115 in arrears, leaving five wickets left for Durham to complete the job.

As the gloom set in after tea, Aldridge uprooted Daz Ahmed's middle stump for a 14-ball duck to register nine wickets in a match for the first time in his career.

With a light reading taken, it seemed only the elements could save Gloucestershire, as first innings half-centurion James Bracey dug in alongside Mitch Killeen.

Carse removed Bracey with a vicious in-swinger - 173-7.

In the 61st over of the innings, light forced Colin Ackermann into the attack, and he struck with his second ball, ending a spirited hand from Killeen to leave his side two wickets away.

Ackermann bowled in partnership with Will Rhodes, while Kishore shone with two sixes in 29.

Ackermann accounted for Hayes, who chipped to mid-wicket and left his side nine down, still trailing by 36.

Kishore and Langdrige had fun against Durham's part-timers, eking out a slender lead with a succession of maximums which ended when Langridge holed out for 36.

Although the umpires returned to the middle, they soon trudged off, and play was called off just after 18:20 BST.

Durham are all but there for a seventh win in 10 games.

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: Michael Vaughan backs Dan Lawrence for run as all-rounder
articles.summary: Former captain Michael Vaughan backs batter Dan Lawrence for a run in England's Test side. How would you solve impending selection headache?
articles.body:
Former captain Michael Vaughan believes Dan Lawrence has shown enough to remain in the England Test side when Jacob Bethell returns from injury.

Lawrence, a batter who bowls part-time off-spin, was a surprise choice when he was picked to fill the role created by the retirement of all-rounder Ben Stokes earlier this summer.

But after making 51 in the first Test at Headingley, Lawrence impressed with 50 not out from 66 balls in tricky conditions on day three of the second Test against Pakistan.

"I think it is a really good selection," Vaughan told BBC Test Match Special. "He will have a period in the England side that we will enjoy watching him bat.

"I think in time his off-spin will come in very handy indeed."

Lawrence impresses as weather delays England

Lawrence hits half-century but rain disrupts England's progress again - as it happened

Lawrence, 29, was recalled after an international absence of almost two years, having averaged 26.84 across 14 previous Tests including a stint as a makeshift opener.

By picking him, England prioritised having four pace bowling options over a frontline spinner, with Lawrence backed to provided the overs of slow bowling if needed. He has only bowled one over in the series so far with pace bowlers dominant.

On Saturday Lawrence made his mark by coming to the crease at 83-4 and steering England to 177-7 in their second innings when rain brought an early close.

The right-hander, whose best Test score remains 91 , countered excessive seam movement and uneven bounce by showing attacking intent, hitting six fours and two sixes.

"He seems to read the game," Vaughan said. "It was the right way to play at that moment.

"He has a quirky technique that has worked for him and is very confident. He knows his scoring areas.

"He is clearly a better player than when he played for England last time."

England's current balance - with Lawrence picked over a frontline spinner - appears suited to home conditions, and could also work in South Africa and Australia where England play this winter.

While stronger spin options would likely be needed for the tour of Bangladesh in the new year, the success of England's pace quartet of Ollie Robinson, Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson and Josh Tongue has lessened the need for a spinner in home conditions and, in turn, helped Lawrence's cause.

Key selection decisions are still looming, however, with Jacob Bethell currently out of the series because of a knee injury.

Bethell, who also bowls part-time spin, could replace Lawrence, or regain his place from Jordan Cox, who has impressed with two fifties while filling in for Bethell at number three.

Other options include pushing Cox or Bethell up to open in place of Emilio Gay - Cox opened early in his career in county cricket and Bethell is England's current 50-over opener - and moving Cox down the order to replace Jamie Smith as wicketkeeper.

Smith scored an impressive 61 in England's first innings and has improved his glovework after a poor showing in the Ashes.

"It's pointless looking to the future because it hasn't happened yet," Lawrence said. "I'm just trying to contribute every Test I can and give a good showing of myself.

"Thankfully, so far, I think I have done.

"Obviously thoughts creep into your head and I'm desperate, along with all the other boys, to establish myself in an England shirt, which is something I haven't quite done in my career so far.

"It's just about trying to take every opportunity you get and really enjoy the occasion instead of feeling nervous about the occasion. Just have fun, play the cricket that's got me here this summer."

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: Dan Lawrence's brilliant 50 lifts hosts to 357-run lead, as rain causes havoc on day three at Lord's
articles.summary: Rain delays caused havoc on day three of the second Test between England and Pakistan at Lord's as Dan Lawrence spurred the hosts on to a lead of 357 striking an impressive half-century; watch day four live on Sky Sports Cricket on Sunday from 10.15am
articles.body:
Lawrence battled hard to acclimatise to the uneven bounce on the Lord's pitch, but would surge to a superb 64-ball half-ton, which included a booming six to long-on, and lead England to a score of 177-7 at stumps.

Intermittent showers delayed proceedings for almost three-and-a-half hours on Saturday morning, with Emilio Gay and Harry Brook eventually taking to the field to bat at 2.20pm.

Mohammad Abbas took full advantage of the conditions, which were highly conducive to the pace bowlers, utilising the pitch's uneven bounce to jag the ball left and right and take impressive figures of 3-48.

Gay and Brook struggle in tricky conditions

Gay's time at the crease would be short-lived, with Abbas pinning the England opener lbw with an unplayable delivery in the second over of the day.

The England batter, who fought brilliantly on Friday evening, will feel hard done by the delivery after the ball skidded off the surface, bouncing low under his bat and onto his back pad.

After another rain delay, Brook (34), who had thought his way through his innings, edged Abbas behind to Mohammad Rizwan standing up to the crease.

It was another excellent piece of bowling from Abbas, who had played his four previous balls down the off side, before coming down much straighter to Brook, jagging the ball away to the off side.

With Rizwan up to the stumps, Brook couldn't get closer to the pitch of the ball and nullify its lateral movement, with the Yorkshireman ultimately edging behind.

While dark clouds loomed low over the Home of Cricket, the rain held off for another four overs before Abbas produced another jaffa to remove Jamie Smith (7).

This time, the ball nipped towards Smith's leg stump, and the wicketkeeper drove forward, pushing an inside edge to Shan Masood, who took the catch comfortably.

An early tea was called as rain began to fall again, but three balls after the break, Pakistan reduced England to 162-7, with Mohammad Ali forcing Gus Atkinson (7) to step across his crease before pinning him on the front pad.

Only 1.5 more overs were bowled before the heavens opened again and the grounds staff raced onto the pitch with the covers.

Fans waited for the players to return to the field and the sun finally broke through the gloom, but farcically, play was abandoned just after 6.30pm due to bad light.

Lawrence and Ollie Robinson (2no) will return to the crease on Sunday for day four.

Fans will be frustrated by bad light decision

Many fans had been left waiting in the stands at Lord's after the players were pulled off the field at 5.08pm due to rain.

The conditions gradually started to improve, but fears arose that both sides would not return to the pitch as the light began to fade.

Just after 6pm, grounds staff began to remove the covers and the sun broke through the clouds.

Both teams needed to be back on the field before 7pm for the match to continue through to the 7.30pm cut-off, and conditions had improved considerably by that point, to the extent that the game could have resumed.

However, the umpires, who have been commended for their efforts to keep play going throughout the opening two Tests, made the decision to abandon the match - a move that will understandably frustrate many of the fans inside the ground, who had already missed more than half a day of cricket due to the weather.

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: Nasser Hussain fumes as day three of second Test at Lord's abandoned during sunshine
articles.summary: Just 24.5 overs possible on Saturday of second Test due to bad light and rain; stumps called at 6.30pm despite sun shining; Dan Lawrence's sixth Test fifty, notched from 64 balls, features stunning six; watch day four from 10.15am, Sunday, Sky Sports Cricket
articles.body:
Just 24.5 overs were possible on a gloomy Saturday due to rain and bad light, during which time England moved from their overnight 81-3 to 177-7 for a lead of 357 as they look to wrap up a series win.

There looked to be a chance of more cricket when the sun began to shine late in the evening, only for the day to be officially called off just after 6.30pm local time, prompting heavy booing from spectators.

Had the players returned to the field before 7pm, play could have been extended to 7.30pm.

On hearing news of the abandonment, Sky Sports expert Hussain said: "That's a joke, honestly a joke. That is an unbelievable decision, it really is.

"These fans have waited here all afternoon for it to stop raining. It is now bright, blue sky in the distance. In about five minutes, it is going to be sunny here."

Speaking moments earlier, after noticing a lack of urgency to get the game on, Hussain said: "I have no idea what's going on and I don't think the fans do.

"It's the brightest it's been for about eight hours. It's not raining - get the covers off and start playing.

"This is the best conditions we have had and no one is doing anything."

'Eye-catching Lawrence got his tempo right'

In the small amount of cricket the fans did see, England's Dan Lawrence clinched a sixth Test half-century with his knock of 50 not out from 66 balls including a stunning six over extra-cover that Sky Sports pundit Dinesh Karthik called "the shot of the series".

Lawrence opted to counter-attack as Pakistan's bowlers found lavish movement and the pitch offered up uneven bounce - his England team-mate Emilio Gay was trapped lbw by Mohammad Abbad from an unplayable delivery that scuttled through low.

On Lawrence's innings, Hussain said: "He got his tempo right. This is not the surface to hang in on, there is a ball with your name on it - as Gay found out - so you have to score, put bowlers under pressure."

Hussain's fellow analyst Stuart Broad added: "Lawrence fought hard and played some eye-catching shots as well.

"He took his time to get in and get used to the pitch and then took it upon himself to put bowlers off their line and length, using his feet."

Lawrence: I'm just trying to contribute in every Test

Lawrence has replaced the retired Ben Stokes in England's XI, recalled after averaging 65.66 for Surrey in the County Championship this term and notching five hundreds.

His Lord's fifty against Pakistan followed a half-century in the series opener at Headingley.

Lawrence is also the chief spin bowling option at the moment as the side go in with an all-pace frontline attack of Jofra Archer, Ollie Robinson, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson.

The 29-year-old said: "I'm just trying to contribute every Test I can and give a good showing of myself. Thankfully, so far, I think I have done.

"I'm desperate, along with all the other boys, to establish myself in an England shirt, which is something I haven't quite done in my career so far.

"It's about trying to take every opportunity you get and really enjoy the occasion instead of feeling nervous. Have fun and play the cricket that's got me here this summer."

articles.title: England v Pakistan: Nasser Hussain calls early end to play at Lord's 'a joke'
articles.summary: The decision to abandon play an hour early after a rain-hit third day of England’s second Test against Pakistan is criticised by former captain Nasser Hussain and fans.
articles.body:
The decision to abandon play an hour before scheduled at the end of the third day of England's second Test against Pakistan was called "a joke" by Nasser Hussain.

On a Saturday badly affected by persistent showers at Lord's, players left the field at 17:08 BST.

At that point, prospects of conditions improving sufficiently for play to resume seemed remote. However, rain cleared and the sky brightened.

The groundstaff partially removed the covers while officials deliberated. At 18:30, with up to an hour of playing time remaining and with the weather the best it had been all day, umpires Paul Reiffel and Allahuddien Parker abandoned proceedings.

The decision was greeted with booing by some of the sparse crowd that remained inside the ground.

"That's a joke, honestly a joke," former England captain Hussain said on Sky Sports.

"I earlier said how good the umpires have been. These fans have waited all afternoon for it to stop raining. It's now bright. There's blue sky in the distance. That is an unbelievable decision, it really is.

"In about five minutes' time it's going to be sunny here."

The weather stayed dry and the light remained good up to 19:30, the time at which play would have been scheduled to close.

The morning session had been washed out and only 24.5 overs of play were possible as the players dodged the showers, meaning spectators will receive a 50% refund on the price of their ticket.

If 30 overs had been completed, spectators would not have been entitled to any money back.

Still, the abandonment caused some fans to express their displeasure with messages to the BBC's live coverage of the Test.

"Sat in the Edrich Stand," wrote Joe at Lord's. "It hasn't rained for half an hour and it's as bright as it's been all day. Absolutely no justification for not playing right now. A real shame."

Rachel in Kingswinford added: "Ridiculous to call it off! They want fans supporting Test cricket and those spectators have stuck with it all day - another 30-45 mins of play would have been a better look (plus saving authorities money on refunds)!"

Another message from Paul in Northwich read: "This is a terrible advert for cricket. It's like the umpires are waiting for it to rain again. At least the spectators can get a refund."

Vaughan backs Lawrence for extended run in England team

Lawrence impresses as weather delays England

Play ended with England 177-7 in their second innings, 357 ahead and on course to win the match and series.

Batting conditions had been difficult all day and it would have been another challenging period for the home side had they been asked to return for a short time late in the evening.

"It would have been a tricky 40 minutes to go out there and bat," said Dan Lawrence, who made an unbeaten 50.

"It's nice to have a good sleep and think about how I'm going to play in the morning. I can imagine it will be with the same intent and trying to push the game forward.

"Forty minutes of batting at 6.45pm is never an ideal thing."

The situation at Lord's came on the same day Durham were denied the chance to chase a victory target of four against Gloucestershire because of bad light at the end of the third day of their County Championship match at Chester-le-Street.

It means the teams will return on Sunday for what could be as little as one ball of action.

Gloucestershire were dismissed for 250 in their second innings in the closing stages of Saturday, with visiting coach Mark Alleyne claiming the light was already too poor before his team were all out.

"I'm not sure where to start, really," said Alleyne. "I mean, 45 minutes before we lost the last wicket, it was too dark to play, which would have been consistent with all the other days that we played."

"We had probably 50 minutes of cricket there that we probably shouldn't have done."

The match could have been concluded had Gloucestershire chosen to bowl spin, only for the away side to refuse and push the game into a Sunday when rain is forecast.

"They asked if we would bowl our spinners to finish the game," added Alleyne. "Of course, we said no, we'll bowl our quick bowlers, in which case it became bad light, so we'll come back tomorrow."

Durham coach Ryan Campbell wrote on X: "Cricket sometimes doesn't help itself. Before everyone loads up on the poor old umpires, it's not their fault."

articles.title: Joe Root: What's behind the England captain's lbw struggles after twice more falling foul at Lord's
articles.summary: Joe Root has been dismissed lbw seven times across five Tests this summer, and nine times in his last 12 Test innings'; watch day four of the seond Test between England and Pakistan at Lord's, live on Sky Sports Cricket from 10.15am on Sunday (play starts 11am)
articles.body:
That was the debate during the rain-interrupted third day's play at Lord's, with the England captain twice succumbing leg before wicket during the second Test against Pakistan - taking his total to seven such dismissals this summer, and nine in his last 12 Test innings.

"It's fascinating that even a guy of more than 160 Tests, who averages over 50 - one of the greatest players England have ever produced - teams will still be looking at that developing trend," Sky Sports Cricket's Michael Atherton said.

"It also reflects how the game is changing. When we started playing, many more bowlers were looking to take the ball away and challenge your outside edge.

"You were taught that Test cricket was played around off stump, or in the channel, and that the best bowlers get the ball to move away, with your danger area the slip cordon.

"What we've seen in recent times in England is bowlers moving to the wobble seam delivery much more, looking to nip the ball back.

"The number of lbws and bowled dismissals this summer is high, and that's how teams will be looking to have a crack at Root. They'll be trying to exploit that slight area of weakness.

"There's also the added context of the wicketkeeper coming up to the stumps to the slower, medium pace bowlers like Matt Henry and Mohammad Abbas - and that is what is keeping Root more in the crease.

"You have more chance of getting that lbw when the keeper is up."

Root's second-innings dismissal to Mohammad Ali came after the Pakistan pacer got one to nip and bounce away from the right-hander, beating the outside edge, the ball before.

Sky Sports Cricket's Nasser Hussain believes it's a contributing factor to Root's lbw struggles, with bowlers managing to set him up with the one that shapes away.

"The moment you see the ball moving away from you, you naturally go to cover the outside edge - Root will go across with that front pad," Hussain said.

"Because the ball is doing so much this summer, any batter will go slightly across with that front leg, as they are worried about the outside edge to the one moving away.

"But as Athers is talking about, the wobble seam then comes into it and nips back - you get four-and-a-quarter inches to cover a ball that's moving away and back in!

"It reminds me a little bit of Terry Alderman, who used to set Graham Gooch up like that: outswing, outswing, outswing, nip back. Goochy had to change his whole technique from back and across, to just back.

"If you watch Root at his best, he is a straight-line sort of batter, back and forward, he stays beside the ball.

"But because the ball is moving so much, he's trying to get across to it and that leaves him vulnerable to the lbw.

"Some of it is due to low bounce as well, especially on this ground [Lord's] - it brings the stumps and lbw into play.

"Bowlers are just holding a length, because they know they will find the stumps.

"And you have to also give the bowlers some credit. The skill we've seen from England, New Zealand, Pakistan this summer to bowl outswing and then wobble seam to bring in the lbw."

And that is Root's dilemma, Atherton added: "Nasser is right, because if Root said to himself, 'I'm going to take the lbw out of the equation and open up a bit', you then become more vulnerable to the outside edge.

"It's what makes this a fascinating game."

articles.title: ‘ I take the blame myself’: Suryakumar Yadav’s big regret over failed ODI career
articles.summary: Cricket News: Suryakumar Yadav has admitted that he only has himself to blame for failing to establish a longer career in ODI cricket, despite becoming one of India.
articles.body: Suryakumar Yadav has admitted that he only has himself to blame for failing to establish a longer career in ODI cricket, despite becoming one of India’s most successful T20 batters.The former India T20I captain played 37 ODIs and scored 773 runs at an average of 25.76, numbers that never quite reflected the impact he had in the shortest format. His final ODI appearance came in the 2023 World Cup final against Australia, and he has not featured in India’s 50-over setup since.Suryakumar, who led India to T20 World Cup glory earlier this year, acknowledged that his ODI career remains a source of disappointment. Rather than pointing to selection calls or circumstances, he accepted responsibility for not doing enough to adapt to the demands of the format.“Hypothetically, we can say anything - that if I had come into the team in 2016, I could have played Tests and probably done well in ODIs too. But the reality is that I played only one Test and one innings. After that, the other players came back and started playing again, so it didn’t happen. But definitely, I am disappointed with myself when it comes to ODI cricket.“It was a white-ball format, just like T20s, but to be very honest, I personally feel I did not put in as much effort as I should have for that format," Suryakumar Yadav said on Aakash Chopra's YouTube channel.Why Suryakumar found ODI cricket difficultWhile T20 cricket has allowed Suryakumar to thrive with his aggressive strokeplay, he believes ODI cricket demands a far more calculated approach from batters.He described the 50-over game as the most difficult format for a batter because situations can change rapidly, particularly for those coming in at No. 4, 5 or 6."I feel ODI cricket is probably the most difficult format to play as a batter, whether you are batting lower down the order or anywhere else. You can be two down for zero if you are batting at No. 4, or four down for 24 if you are batting at No. 6. Anything can happen. You have to bat almost like you do in a Test match. You see off the bowlers initially, give them respect and slowly build your innings. You may bat at a strike rate of 50 or sometimes 75, then take it to 100 and eventually finish at 130 or 140, much like you do in T20 cricket," he added.According to Suryakumar, the challenge was not simply about batting in a different format. He struggled to work out exactly how he needed to construct an innings in ODI cricket, particularly in the middle order.'I did not put in the extra effort'Suryakumar revealed that he knew he was likely to occupy a middle-order role, but failed to put the same level of preparation into ODI cricket that he now gives T20 cricket.“Personally, I feel I could not crack how to approach that format. I knew I was probably going to bat at No. 5 or 6, but even then, I did not work hard enough to understand the format. By the time I could blink, those 20-25 games had gone. I don’t even know when it happened or how it went by. And yes, I definitely regret not playing more ODI cricket. I wonder why I could not do better in that format. But no one is to blame. I take the blame myself because I did not put in the extra effort that I put in now when I play T20 cricket. If I bat for an hour, I will practise for an hour and a half," he said.Suryakumar's ODI career therefore remains one of the unfinished chapters of his international journey. Despite making a major impact in T20 cricket, he could not translate that success into the 50-over format before his run in the ODI side came to an end after the 2023 World Cup final.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘He does not depend on the pitch’: Rahane explains why Manav Suthar can thrive anywhere
articles.summary: Cricket News: Manav Suthar has wasted little time making an impression in Test cricket, with the left-arm spinner already putting himself in the conversation for a .
articles.body: Manav Suthar has wasted little time making an impression in Test cricket, with the left-arm spinner already putting himself in the conversation for a bigger role in India’s red-ball plans.Suthar has claimed 23 wickets from his first three Tests, but his impact has gone beyond the numbers. His ability to generate drift, combine it with a deceptive release and consistently hit the right areas has made him an awkward proposition for batters.Ajinkya Rahane has been particularly impressed by the early signs from the youngster. The former India captain believes Suthar’s biggest strength could be his ability to remain effective without relying heavily on assistance from the pitch."I have noticed two things about Manav. The first thing is that for him, the pitch does not matter, whether it turns or not. His speed through the air helps him deceive the batters. It is important and good that you do not depend on the wicket as a spinner. Then you can do well in any condition. The other thing was the way he altered the speed. He has been a quick learner in just three games. He bowled differently to each batter and used the angles well. Yes, it is early, but he has done well," he said in a video on his Hindi YouTube Channel.Suthar making a case for bigger roleThe 23 wickets in three matches have given Suthar an impressive beginning to his international career, while his adaptability has added another dimension to his prospects.Suthar’s early performances have already established him as India’s lead spinner. Even during the Sri Lanka tour, he was captain Shubman Gill’s first choice whenever the team needed wickets. Since Ravindra Jadeja is gradually becoming more of a batting all-rounder—especially in overseas conditions, Suthar is expected to be India's leading spinner for the near future.His ability to adjust his pace, angles and approach according to the batter has particularly stood out, strengthening the argument that he can be effective across different conditions.Rahane warns India of New Zealand challengeRahane also turned his attention to India’s next Test assignment in New Zealand, where the conditions are expected to be considerably different from those the team experienced in Sri Lanka.The former India batter believes adapting quickly to the conditions will be central to India’s preparations. He also highlighted the value of match practice ahead of a challenging series."The conditions will be totally different in New Zealand. You need to read the wicket and adapt that way. In the last five to six years, we have seen that the team adapts well. I expect them to prepare well. The good thing was that they played a practice match in Sri Lanka. If they get the time for that in New Zealand too, it will be very crucial for mental and physical preparation, even skill-wise," he expressed.For Suthar, however, the immediate task is to build on an encouraging start. Three Tests and 23 wickets have already given him a platform, while his ability to produce results without depending solely on turning pitches could prove valuable as India look to strengthen their spin options for the future.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: Joe Root has added another major record to his remarkable Test career, surpassing Ricky Ponting to become the highest run-scorer in Test history on home soil.The England captain reached the milestone during the second Test against Pakistan at Lord's in London. Root came to the crease on Day 2 and made 24 before Pakistan pacer Mohammad Ali dismissed him lbw.Although Root was unable to turn the start into a substantial innings, those 24 runs were enough to take him past Ponting's long-standing mark.Root now has 7,594 Test runs in England, moving ahead of Ponting's 7,578 runs accumulated in Australia. India's Sachin Tendulkar occupies third place on the list, having scored 7,216 Test runs in India.Root moves past PontingRoot's latest achievement adds another landmark to a career that has already seen him climb to the top of several major Test batting charts.The England star has reached his 7,594 home runs in 89 Tests and 156 innings, averaging 53.85. His record includes 24 centuries and 35 fifties, with a highest score of 254.Ponting finished his home career with 7,578 runs from 92 Tests and 154 innings at an average of 56.97. The former Australia captain registered 23 hundreds and 38 fifties, with a best of 257.Tendulkar is next on the list with 7,216 runs from 94 Tests and 153 innings in India, while Mahela Jayawardene and Jacques Kallis complete the top five.PlayerCountryTime spanMatchesInningsRunsBest scoreAverage100s50sJoe RootEngland2013-202689156759425453.852435Ricky PontingAustralia1995-201292154757825756.972338Sachin TendulkarIndia1990-201394153721621752.672232Mahela JayawardeneSri Lanka1997-201481129716737459.722334Jacques KallisSouth Africa1995-201388143703522456.732334Tendulkar's all-time record next?Root's record-breaking run at home has also brought renewed attention to another major milestone that remains within his reach.The England batter is currently 1,713 runs behind Tendulkar's all-time Test record of 15,921 runs. Root has scored 14,208 runs in 168 Test matches, while Tendulkar remains at the top of the overall chart.The question of whether Root can eventually overhaul the Indian legend's record is no longer a matter of "if," but "when."England maintain control at Lord'sRoot's latest milestone came as England continued to hold a commanding position in the second Test against Pakistan, although rain severely restricted the third day's action at Lord's.England reached 177-7 by the close of a disrupted Day 3, taking their overall lead to 357 runs. Only 24.5 overs were possible after showers prevented play during the morning session.The hosts eventually returned in the afternoon with England on 81-3. Dan Lawrence went on to race to an unbeaten 50 from 66 balls before another spell of rain arrived just 14 balls after the teams resumed following tea.There was no further play, with the day eventually abandoned at 6.30pm local time because of bad light.England lost four wickets while adding 96 runs. Emilio Gay was dismissed for 31, Harry Brook fell for 34 and Jamie Smith made seven, with Mohammad Abbas claiming all three wickets to finish the innings with 3-48. Gus Atkinson was then trapped lbw for seven by Mohammad Ali.Lawrence remained unbeaten on 50 alongside Ollie Robinson, who was on two at the close.England had earlier made 290 in their first innings before bowling Pakistan out for 110.The hosts won the opening Test at Headingley by an innings last week and are now looking to seal the three-match series against Pakistan.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'That's a joke': Nasser Hussain slams umpires' decision to abandon England vs Pakistan Day 3 at Lord's
articles.summary: Cricket News: The decision to end play early on the third day of England’s second Test against Pakistan at Lord’s has sparked criticism after the weather improved s.
articles.body: The decision to end play early on the third day of England’s second Test against Pakistan at Lord’s has sparked criticism after the weather improved soon after the umpires called it off.Rain had disrupted most of Saturday, with the morning session completely washed out and only 24.5 overs possible. Players left the field at 17:08 BST, when conditions still looked poor. But the rain soon stopped, the sky became brighter and ground staff began removing some of the covers.Despite this, umpires Paul Reiffel and Allahuddien Parker abandoned the day at 18:30, with around an hour of scheduled play still available. Some fans booed the decision, while former England captain Nasser Hussain strongly criticised it."That's a joke, honestly a joke," former England captain Hussain said on Sky Sports."I earlier said how good the umpires have been. These fans have waited all afternoon for it to stop raining. It's now bright. There's blue sky in the distance. That is an unbelievable decision, it really is."In about five minutes' time it's going to be sunny here."The weather stayed dry until the scheduled close at 19:30. Because fewer than 30 overs were played, spectators will receive a 50% ticket refund.England in control as debate continuesEngland finished the day on 177-7, holding a 357-run lead and looking well placed to win the match and series. Dan Lawrence, unbeaten on 50, said returning for only 40 minutes would not have been ideal."It would have been a tricky 40 minutes to go out there and bat," said Dan Lawrence, who made an unbeaten 50."It's nice to have a good sleep and think about how I'm going to play in the morning. I can imagine it will be with the same intent and trying to push the game forward."Forty minutes of batting at 6.45pm is never an ideal thing."The controversy came alongside a similar situation in the County Championship, where Durham were unable to chase four runs against Gloucestershire because of bad light.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘CoE cannot be only for contracted players’: VVS Laxman on building India’s cricket pipeline
articles.summary: Cricket News: Bengaluru: Giving up a lucrative IPL contract and a thriving commentary career, Indian batting great VVS Laxman took the administrative plunge in Dece.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Giving up a lucrative IPL contract and a thriving commentary career, Indian batting great VVS Laxman took the administrative plunge in December 2021. What began at a modest facility inside the M Chinnaswamy Stadium has since evolved into a much larger assignment, with Laxman now at the helm of the BCCI Centre of Excellence, the state-of-the-art facility on the outskirts of the city.The Hyderabadi, whose playing career was defined by wristy elegance and remarkable resilience, is set to complete his tenure later this year.In an exclusive interview with TOI, Laxman reflects on his journey at the CoE, the changing landscape of Indian cricket and the pathways through which the game can transition, evolve and transform.ExcerptsFrom a compact facility at the M Chinnaswamy Stadium to the expansive centre, how has the journey been?It has been a very fulfilling journey. When I started in late December 2021, we were working with a relatively small facility, and today we have a much larger and more comprehensive Centre of Excellence. The then BCCI secretary and current ICC chairman, Jay Shah, deserves tremendous credit for having the vision to invest in this facility and create an ecosystem of this scale. I am also grateful to the leadership for giving me the freedom and trust to develop and execute the vision we had for the CoE.What, according to you, has been the biggest change?For me, the biggest change is not just the infrastructure but also the ecosystem we have built around it, bringing together coaching, sports science, technology and education.While contracted players benefit from the facility, how has it been working with domestic players, giving them more access to technology, quality coaching, and support staff?This is extremely important to the BCCI. The CoE cannot be only for contracted players. If we want to strengthen Indian cricket, we have to strengthen the pathway beneath the international level as well. We are therefore trying to give domestic and pathway players greater access to quality coaching, sports science, performance analysis and technology. The idea is to identify potential early and give players the right environment to develop. Ultimately, CoE should contribute to the entire Indian cricket ecosystem, not just one particular group of players.Active players have now started taking a keen interest in coaching and are going through the coaching courses. What do you attribute this trend to?It is a very encouraging trend. Players who have played at the first-class or international level have enormous knowledge and experience, and naturally many of them want to give something back to the game. But playing and coaching are two different skill sets. That is why coach education is important. We help them understand communication, planning, leadership and most importantly, how to transfer their experience to another player. More players are now recognising that their impact on the game can continue well beyond their playing careers.Are there any sessions for them to mentally transition from players to coaches?It’s not one session; it’s an ongoing mentoring process. Transition from player to coach doesn’t happen overnight. It is really a change in mindset. As a player, your primary responsibility is your own performance. As a coach, your responsibility is to make other people better. Through our coaching courses, we expose former and current players to communication, leadership, planning, managing different personalities and understanding individual players. The biggest learning is that coaching is not about showing people how much you know, but it is about helping the player discover how much they can achieve.Can you put down in numbers the high performance camps that CoE conducts across the country in a year?The scale of our high performance work has grown significantly. Throughout the year, we run programmes across the pathway for both men and women players from the U-16, U-19, and U-23 age groups, as well as targeted specialist skill camps, including fast and spin bowler camps. We now directly support more than 150 players annually, and the impact is clear in the outcomes we are seeing: improved skill levels, stronger readiness for international cricket, and more players progressing successfully through the pathway into higher levels. Our objective is to create a continuous pathway from age group cricket right through to international level.The setting up of the women’s coaching system -- what’s that process been like?It has been a very exciting process because women’s cricket in India has grown tremendously. The support ecosystem has to grow at the same pace. We are working on a more structured system around women’s cricket. We are also investing in developing coaches and support staff. Importantly, we don’t want to copy the men’s system. Women’s cricket has its own requirements, and we need to develop expertise around those specific needs.How much have you enjoyed watching youngsters bloom from CoE, especially the U-19 players with whom you spend a considerable amount of time?That is one of the most rewarding parts of my role. When you see a young player come into the CoE with potential and then watch him develop not just as a cricketer but also as a person, it gives you enormous satisfaction. With U-19 players, you are dealing with an important stage of their development. You are not just preparing them for the next tournament; you are trying to give them the habits, discipline, resilience, and awareness for a long career. When you subsequently see them progress into India A or senior cricket, it is incredibly satisfying.For somebody who's in a mentorship role, since you've travelled so much with the under-19s and the A-teams, what is that one thing that you tell them?So with the under-19s or the A-teams, it's about getting better every day as a player in every aspect of their game. So it's not only about skill, but the mental aspect, the physical aspect, and how they can improve, because at the end of the day, any sport you play, any match you play, if you don't have that competitive spirit, then you're not a sports person.So you go out there to perform, you go out there to win the match and win the series, but at the same time, whether it's with under-19s or with the India players, it's also about measuring objectively how you're progressing after every match.It’s satisfying when you see that progress in a player because the whole endeavour is: Can they reach a stage where they can win matches for the senior Indian team in any international fixture and also perform at the highest level?There has been a lot of focus on camps in the North East; can you elaborate?The domestic circuit and structure is so robust, and there are so many matches happening across the different age groups. There's a lot of emphasis on developing the talent in the North-East.So we have camps which are dedicated to the North-East players, men and women from U-19 to senior age group. It’s great to see that every year the quality of those players has definitely gotten better, and the only way it will get better is if they get more exposure.How do they get more exposure?By playing against good teams. You test yourself and gain confidence only when you play against good teams and do well; that's how they get exposure.How has the introduction of the U-15 category for women helped in identifying players?We started it three years ago. It allows us to strengthen the bench and see players develop. We have players from the first batch who went on to play for India. G Kamalini was in the first batch of the U-15 tournament, and she played for India. So it's great to see not only the boys, but also the girls, benefiting from the various tournaments and camps we run under the BCCI umbrella.When you switch roles from administrator to mentor coach, does it help that you see these players up close as an administrator?Coaching and mentoring come naturally because, as an India player, my interactions with the youngsters were always very seamless and holistic. You share your experiences, help them evolve and develop as cricketers, and maximise their potential.The administration part is obviously a different experience, and luckily again, the structures in the BCCI system made that seamless as well. The best part of this role is getting to see so many players come, perform, get selected, attend the camps, and repeat the process the next year.So it's great to see some of the players who were attending the U-19 camps in 2022 playing for India in 2025-26.When you look back at the almost five years of your journey at NCA/CoE, what’s the most satisfying aspect?The most satisfying thing has been seeing the ecosystem come together. It is not about one facility or one individual. It is about coaches, SSM professionals, performance analysts, grounds staff, administrators and players all working towards the same objective. I am particularly proud that the CoE has evolved into a place where players don’t come only when they are injured. They come to develop their skills, improve physically, learn and become better cricketers.The most fulfilling part of this journey as the CoE head of cricket has been seeing the players' transformation, and we hope they've now achieved their dream and will continue to bring laurels to the country.Ultimately, the real success will be when these systems continue to benefit Indian cricket for many years to come.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Tilak Varma in India’s ODI World Cup plans as selectors seek Shreyas Iyer backup
articles.summary: Cricket News: New Delhi: India’s team management and selectors are working on backups for the middle order ahead of the ODI World Cup next year. TOI has learnt that.
articles.body: New Delhi: India’s team management and selectors are working on backups for the middle order ahead of the ODI World Cup next year. TOI has learnt that Tilak Varma’s name has come up as a potential backup option for Shreyas Iyer in the top six of the batting lineup.Tilak, being a left-handed batter, is seen as someone who can break the monotony of right-handers in the batting lineup. Tilak has been asked to work on his bowling since it is believed that his off-breaks have a lot of potential. The team management, in fact, has flagged the dearth of bowling options in the top order, citing it as a reason for extra pressure on the lower order and the bowlers.The planning for the ODI World Cup will only begin in earnest when India reach New Zealand in October, since most of the first-choice players will not be available for the ODI series against West Indies at home from September 27. A full-strength T20 team is also scheduled to travel to Japan for the Asian Games at the same time.“Head coach Gautam Gambhir and captain Shubman Gill feel there isn’t any backup ready for the middle order. With Hardik Pandya and Nitish Kumar Reddy being prone to injuries, they want someone in the top order who can at least chip in with four overs in an ODI,” a BCCI source said.Over the last year, the team management has been compelled to play either Washington Sundar or Axar Patel at No. 5 or No. 6 to balance the playing XI. In the last series in England, Ishan Kishan was sent in ahead of vice-captain Iyer.“The team has to be prepared for conditions in South Africa in the World Cup. Iyer got injured in Australia and his game against pace and bounce is untested of late. The team already has two ageing players in Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli. They are having niggles as well. KL Rahul too will be over 35 by the time the World Cup comes around. Ravindra Jadeja isn’t a certainty either. The fielding of the team has suffered due to fitness issues. The team management feels that they need younger backups ready,” the source said.Selectors wary of moving batters aroundThe selectors, it is learnt, are not comfortable with playing batters out of position. Last year, Ruturaj Gaikwad was played at No. 4 and scored a hundred against South Africa in Raipur. But he has not been picked in the ODI team since.“Gaikwad was picked as backup opener since Gill was injured. The team management feels Tilak could have been tried in that place. That’s why they don’t want to rush Devdutt Padikkal in the ODI setup because he found his calling in white-ball cricket while opening the batting,” the source said.The team for the West Indies series, however, will be an anomaly since Iyer, Tilak, Ishan and Axar will not be available. The selectors are more focused on picking another wicketkeeper for the series.Team for Afg series likely by Sept 3The selection committee is due to meet by September 3 to pick the team for the three-match T20I series against Afghanistan in Delhi from September 13.Sources said that the selectors are likely to retain the team selected for the subsequent Asian Games. The official fitness reports of Hardik, Nitish Reddy and Jasprit Bumrah are awaited. Varun Chakravarthy has regained full fitness, it is learnt.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Aise bhi log hote hain life mein’: Suryakumar reveals Sanju Samson’s incredible response after being dropped
articles.summary: Cricket News: Suryakumar Yadav has opened up on one of the most difficult decisions he made during India’s title-winning 2026 T20 World Cup campaign, revealing how .
articles.body: Suryakumar Yadav has opened up on one of the most difficult decisions he made during India’s title-winning 2026 T20 World Cup campaign, revealing how Sanju Samson responded when he was left out of the playing XI.Samson entered the tournament struggling for form and did not initially feature in India’s plans. Ishan Kishan had impressed at the top during the series against New Zealand and was preferred ahead of him, leaving Samson to wait for his opportunity.But India’s slow start to the World Cup, coupled with Abhishek Sharma not being fully fit and the team's struggles against off-spin, eventually brought Samson back into contention. Once given the chance, the wicketkeeper-batter completely transformed his campaign.Samson produced crucial back-to-back performances in the knockout stages to help India win the World Cup and was subsequently named Player of the Tournament. He finished with 321 runs in five innings at an average of 80.25, while his strike rate of 199.38 underlined the impact he made during India's title-winning campaign.Suryakumar reveals Samson's responseSuryakumar, who captained India during the tournament, recalled speaking to Samson after the decision to leave him out.Rather than expressing frustration, Samson told his captain that he would continue preparing as though he were going to play and would be ready whenever the team needed him."We were on the bus, and I told him that it was going to be difficult with how it was going. He told me just one thing: do whatever you feel is right to make this team win the World Cup. He said he is there whenever I need him, as he will prepare as if he were going to play. I gained a lot of confidence hearing that. Aise bhi log hote hain life mein (There are people like this too)," Suryakumar said on Aakash Chopra's YouTube channel.For Suryakumar, the decision was particularly difficult because he had previously backed Samson during a lean period and assured him that he would receive an extended run.'That was my toughest call'The former India captain recalled Samson's struggles during the 2024 tour of Sri Lanka, when the batter failed to score heavily before seeking advice from Suryakumar during the Duleep Trophy in Anantapur.Suryakumar said he and the coach had confidence in Samson and promised him a long run in the side."That was my toughest call because I knew that he was a good person. We went to Sri Lanka in 2024, and he did not score a lot of runs there. He asked me what he should do. We were playing the Duleep Trophy in Anantapur. I told him I had confidence in him and that the coach had shown it as well. I assured him that he would play the next seven matches, and even if he scored seven ducks, he would still play the eighth," he added.The faith eventually appeared justified on the biggest stage. Samson went from being outside the XI at the start of the World Cup to becoming one of India's most important players in the knockout rounds.From World Cup hero to uncertain futureSamson's situation has once again become complicated after the World Cup. The IPL took place after the T20 World Cup, and Samson enjoyed a productive campaign, scoring 477 runs across 13 innings at an average of 47.7. Yet his strong IPL season has not translated into a secure place in India's T20I setup.After just three failures on the Ireland and England tour, Samson was dropped from the playing XI and was also not included in India's squad for the Zimbabwe tour. He did, however, feature in the fifth and final T20I against England.His immediate future with the national side remains uncertain, although he has been included in India's squad for the upcoming Asian Games.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: Bengaluru: The 2026-27 domestic season is barely underway, but the old North-South rivalry is already adding spice to the Duleep Trophy. North Zone and South Zone will renew their contest in the semifinals at the BCCI Centre of Excellence here from Sunday, with youth and experience on both sides making for an intriguing battle.North bring the exuberance of youth, with the likes of Ayush Doseja keen to build on early promise. South, runners-up in the last edition, have a blend of emerging talent and established names, with Karnataka youngster R Smaran joining the likes of Tilak Varma and Karun Nair.On paper, the contest could boil down to South’s formidable batting against North’s in-form bowling. Smaran, the leading run-scorer in last season’s Ranji Trophy with 950 runs, will be one of South’s key batters, while captain Tilak, Karun and Narayan Jagadeesan give the side considerable depth.When the two sides met in the previous edition, South had the upper hand, with Jagadeesan’s 197 helping them secure a sizeable first-innings lead before they eventually marched into the final.This time, however, South will have to contend with a North attack brimming with confidence. Left-arm spinner Abid Mushtaq was instrumental in their quarterfinal win over West Zone, claiming nine wickets. If the surface offers turn, Mushtaq and Nishant Sindhu could pose a serious challenge to South’s batting.Will Vaibhav make a statement?For East Zone’s Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, the other semifinal against defending champions Central Zone offers another opportunity to make a statement in red-ball cricket.The 15-year-old southpaw managed a single-digit score against Northeast Zone in the quarterfinal and will be eager to make a bigger contribution this time. Central, meanwhile, will be led by Rajat Patidar, setting up another strategic test for Sooryavanshi.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ‘Please, let’s not’: Gavaskar rejects free-hit idea in Tests after India’s no-ball problem
articles.summary: Cricket News: Sunil Gavaskar has rejected the idea of introducing free hits in Test cricket to tackle the growing problem of no-balls, insisting that batters should.
articles.body: Sunil Gavaskar has rejected the idea of introducing free hits in Test cricket to tackle the growing problem of no-balls, insisting that batters should not be handed an easier route to scoring runs in the longest format.The debate emerged after India were unable to complete a 2-0 sweep against Sri Lanka in the second Test in Colombo. Shubman Gill's side needed only four wickets on the final day to seal victory, but Sonal Dinusha's unbeaten century helped Sri Lanka survive and force a draw.India still secured a 1-0 series win and kept their hopes of reaching the World Test Championship final alive. However, the number of no-balls bowled by India's spinners during the series has raised concerns.Ravindra Jadeja repeatedly overstepped during the two Tests. The senior left-arm spinner has bowled more than 85 no-balls since 2021, while debutant Saransh Jain also delivered several no-balls during the second innings in Colombo.The issue prompted India's spin bowling coach Sairaj Bahutule to suggest, albeit jokingly, that free hits could be introduced in Test cricket to discourage bowlers from overstepping.Gavaskar, however, believes such a move would punish the wrong side. The former India captain argued that no-balls are one of the few aspects of cricket completely within a player's control and said the problem needs to be addressed immediately because repeated errors can have a major impact on a Test match."The no-balls being bowled by the Indian bowlers came in for a fair bit of comment. This has to be looked at urgently because it can change the colour of the game. There are very few aspects of the game that are totally in the players' control, and a batter taking guard and a bowler not bowling a no-ball are two such aspects. Players, when they come for interviews, talk about doing things within their control. Today, with a tape measure available to mark the run-up, there should be no excuses for overstepping the bowling crease," Gavaskar wrote in his column for Mid-Day.Gavaskar rejects free-hit ideaGavaskar was equally clear in opposing the proposal to give batters a free hit after a no-ball in Test cricket.He pointed out that scoring has already become somewhat easier because of the restrictions on bouncers and the shorter boundaries, and believes introducing another advantage for batters would go too far.“The India team spinning coach jokingly said that giving a free hit after a no-ball might help in curbing the offence. Please, let’s not make scoring runs in Test cricket easier for batters with this penalty. As it is, with the restriction on bouncers to two in an over and the boundaries being brought in, run-making has become a little simpler,” he added.Instead of changing the rules of the game, Gavaskar believes financial penalties could provide a stronger deterrent.His proposal is straightforward: players should be fined whenever they overstep the crease, with the punishment increasing each time the offence is repeated. He also believes the bowling coach should share some responsibility.“Instead, how about a fine which gets doubled for every further transgression, plus half the amount of the fine for the bowling coach, too. The fines collected can be used for the final team dinner before the boys disperse," wrote Gavaskar.Gavaskar suggests more team finesThe former India captain also suggested expanding the idea beyond no-balls, with the team itself having a say in deciding whether certain on-field mistakes deserve penalties.He cited instances such as failing to back up a throw as examples of errors that could be included. Gavaskar believes such an approach could turn fines into a light-hearted team activity while also encouraging greater accountability."There could be other fines too, for example, not backing up for a throw or something else not done on the field, which the whole team can vote on whether to impose or not. This can also be a fun activity and bond the team even more,” he added.India's inability to finish off Sri Lanka in Colombo ultimately denied them a clean sweep, but Gavaskar's concern goes beyond the result. With Test matches often decided by fine margins, he believes avoidable no-balls are an issue India must address rather than compensate for by giving batters another scoring opportunity.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Pakistan chapter I had before is now closed': Mohammad Amir calls himself 'British local'
articles.summary: Cricket News: Mohammad Amir has ended speculation over a possible return to Pakistan's national team, confirming that his international career is now firmly behind .
articles.body: Mohammad Amir has ended speculation over a possible return to Pakistan's national team, confirming that his international career is now firmly behind him.The left-arm pacer, who retired from international cricket in December 2024, has obtained British citizenship and a British passport through his wife, Narjis Khan.Amir explained that his new status means he can no longer be treated as a local Pakistani player in competitions such as the County Championship and The Hundred. Players registered as locals in English domestic cricket must declare that they will not represent another country as a local player."I am a British local now. When you play in competitions such as the County Championship and The Hundred as a local player, you have to sign a document stating that you cannot play for another country as a local. So, the Pakistan chapter I had before is now closed," Amir said in an interview with cricket YouTuber Furqan Bhatti.Amir represented Pakistan in 36 Tests, 61 ODIs and 62 T20Is, taking 119, 81 and 71 wickets respectively. He also played in three World Cups, including the 2019 ODI World Cup, where he was Pakistan's leading wicket-taker with 17 wickets.A career remembered for big momentsAmir played important roles in Pakistan's 2009 T20 World Cup and 2017 Champions Trophy triumphs. His most memorable performance came in the 2017 Champions Trophy final against India, where he took 3-16 and dismissed Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli and Shikhar Dhawan. Pakistan went on to win by 180 runs.He also impressed at the 2019 World Cup, taking a five-wicket haul against Australia.While his decision may disappoint supporters who hoped to see him return for the 2027 World Cup, Amir's international career already includes several unforgettable performances. His move to British citizenship allows him to extend his career in county and franchise cricket, while his achievements for Pakistan remain a major part of his legacy.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates.
