articles.title: Imran Khan went from leading Pakistan to its greatest cricket triumph in 1992 to becoming the country’s prime minister, but now remains behind bars while facing more than 100 cases
articles.summary: Cricket News: Imran Khan’s prison conditions have become the centre of a fresh controversy involving Pakistan cricket, after his sons raised concerns about his heal.
articles.body: Imran Khan’s prison conditions have become the centre of a fresh controversy involving Pakistan cricket, after his sons raised concerns about his health in an interview with former England captain Michael Atherton.The interview, featuring Khan’s sons Sulaiman and Kasim, was broadcast by Sky Sports during the lunch break on Day 1 of the second Test between England and Pakistan at Lord’s. The programme triggered a strong reaction from the Pakistan Cricket Board, with reports suggesting the Pakistan team had even considered refusing to return to the field if the interview was aired.The threat ultimately amounted to talks rather than action. Meanwhile, Pakistan’s government broadcaster PTV, which was carrying Sky Sports’ feed, reportedly switched to advertisements when the interview preview went on air rather than showing the segment.Khan’s sons raise health concernsKasim and Sulaiman spoke about what they described as deteriorating conditions for their father, who has been imprisoned since 2023. Kasim alleged that the situation had become so serious that he believed the authorities were deliberately trying to keep Khan isolated and “blatantly trying to kill him”.Kasim claimed Khan had lost around 80 per cent of the vision in one eye and had recently been seen wearing an eye patch. He also alleged that the former Pakistan prime minister spends more than 23 hours a day alone in a small prison cell, with limited access to books and basic comforts.“They are not even acting with any kind of strategy any more. It is not very clear what they are doing, just blatantly trying to kill him in there. Keep him in as long as possible, and silence him,” Kasim said.He claimed Khan had told relatives that the conditions had severely worsened and that he was being increasingly isolated, comparing his situation with other political prisoners who had died in custody.Kasim also described his father as visibly stressed, saying the change was particularly worrying because Khan had always appeared calm even in dangerous situations.Why the hospital visit became controversialThe concerns came shortly after Pakistan’s Supreme Court directed that Khan be taken for a medical examination.His sons said they had initially been cautiously optimistic that he would receive proper treatment at a private hospital. Instead, they claimed he was taken to a government medical facility for a short examination before being returned to prison.“We were cautiously optimistic. Our fears were confirmed when, instead of being taken to the private hospital, where he was meant to be taken, he was just taken to a government medical facility for a few hours, and then taken straight back to jail,” Sulaiman said.He claimed Khan was examined for about an hour by government officials before being sent back to prison, despite doctors waiting for him at Shifa International Hospital.Khan was subsequently taken to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad on August 21 for a medical check-up before being returned to Adiala jail in accordance with the Supreme Court's orders.Former cricketers interveneThe latest controversy has also drawn former cricketers into the debate.A group of former international captains, including Indian greats Sunil Gavaskar and Kapil Dev, wrote to Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif urging authorities to ensure that Khan receives proper medical treatment and humane conditions in prison.The appeal was framed as a humanitarian intervention rather than a political statement.Former England captain Michael Atherton, who interviewed Khan’s sons for Sky Sports, had also previously joined calls for greater attention to the former Pakistan captain’s health.Why has Imran Khan been in jail?Imran Khan’s imprisonment stems from a series of legal cases that followed his removal as Pakistan’s prime minister in April 2022.On April 10, 2022, Pakistan’s National Assembly removed Khan through a no-confidence vote, making him the first Pakistani prime minister to be ousted through such a motion. Khan subsequently began a political campaign against the government, alleging that the military and his political opponents had worked together to remove him.His legal troubles escalated over the following year.In August 2022, Khan was booked under Pakistan’s anti-terrorism law and later secured protective bail from the Islamabad High Court. In October 2022, the Election Commission of Pakistan disqualified him from contesting elections for five years after finding him guilty of concealing details related to the sale of gifts received from foreign leaders.Arrests and Toshakhana casesKhan was arrested on May 9, 2023, in connection with the Toshakhana case. The arrest triggered violent protests by his supporters across Pakistan.The Islamabad High Court subsequently ordered his release, but he was arrested again in August 2023 after being sentenced to three years in prison in the Toshakhana case.His legal troubles continued into 2024. In January, Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi were handed a separate 14-year sentence in another Toshakhana case. The Islamabad High Court later suspended that sentence in April 2024.Khan and Bushra Bibi were also sentenced to seven years each in February 2024 in the case concerning their 2018 marriage, commonly referred to as the iddat case. They were acquitted in July 2024.Although Khan secured bail in another graft case in November 2024, he remained in jail because of other cases against him.Al-Qadir Trust convictionThe latest major conviction came on January 17, 2025, when Khan was sentenced to 14 years in prison in the Al-Qadir Trust land case. Bushra Bibi was sentenced to seven years in the same case.The case centred on allegations that Khan and Bushra Bibi received land through the Al-Qadir Trust, a charitable trust they established in 2018. Pakistani authorities alleged that the land was linked to a settlement involving property developer Malik Riaz and was worth up to $25 million.Khan has faced legal proceedings in more than 100 cases since his removal from office.From cricket hero to prime ministerLong before entering politics, Khan was one of Pakistan’s biggest sporting icons.As captain, he led Pakistan to its first ODI World Cup title in 1992. Four years later, in 1996, he founded the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.PTI failed to win a seat in the 1997 general election, but Khan won the party’s only seat in the 2002 election.His political rise continued over the next decade before he became Pakistan’s prime minister in August 2018.Khan remained prime minister until April 2022, when he was removed through a no-confidence vote. His fall from power was followed by a series of legal cases, arrests and convictions that eventually led to his continued imprisonment.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.summary: Cricket News: Teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi took on a new responsibility on Sunday as he captained East Zone for the first time in senior first-class crick.
articles.body: Teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi took on a new responsibility on Sunday as he captained East Zone for the first time in senior first-class cricket during their Duleep Trophy semifinal against Central Zone.15-year-old Sooryavanshi, who is normally East Zone's vice-captain, stepped in after regular skipper Ishan Kishan was forced off the field with a thumb injury while keeping wickets. Kumar Kushagra replaced Kishan behind the stumps, while Sooryavanshi temporarily took charge of the team.Sooryavanshi embraces leadership roleThe youngster has been one of the talking points of East Zone's Duleep Trophy campaign. Although he managed only eight runs in the quarter-final against North East Zone, he impressed with the ball by taking two wickets.Sooryavanshi later spoke about his experience of bowling and taking responsibility for the team."If you ask any batter, they always enjoy bowling. A batter always enjoys bowling and a bowler always enjoys batting equally," Sooryavanshi said in a video posted by BCCI Domestic.The teenager also revealed that Kishan took a chance by giving him the ball and described himself as a "wicket-taker"."Opponent team's wickets weren't falling, so I was asked to bowl two or three overs. Ishan Bhaiya felt like he was taking a risk, but he didn't know that I am a wicket-taker," he added.East Zone make strong startEast Zone won the toss and chose to bowl first against Rajat Patidar's Central Zone. Saransh Jain returned to the Central lineup after recently making his India debut in the Colombo Test against Sri Lanka.East's bowlers made an early impact, restricting Central to 81/3 after 32 overs in the opening session. Abhijit K Sarkar claimed two wickets, while Mukesh Kumar took one.Sarkar dismissed Aman Mokhade and Kunal Chandela early, before Mukesh removed Central captain Patidar. Mohammed Shami also kept Patidar under pressure during an intense contest as East Zone controlled the opening session.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body:
Bengaluru: Giving up a lucrative IPL contract and a thriving commentary career, Indian batting great VVS Laxman took the administrative plunge in December 2021. What began at a modest facility inside the M Chinnaswamy Stadium has since evolved into a much larger assignment, with Laxman now at the helm of the BCCI Centre of Excellence, the state-of-the-art facility on the outskirts of the city. The Hyderabadi, whose playing career was defined by wristy elegance and remarkable resilience, is set to complete his tenure later this year. In an exclusive interview with TOI, Laxman reflects on his journey at the CoE, the changing landscape of Indian cricket and the pathways through which the game can transition, evolve and transform. Excerpts

From a compact facility at the M Chinnaswamy Stadium to the expansive centre, how has the journey been?

It has been a very fulfilling journey. When I started in late December 2021, we were working with a relatively small facility, and today we have a much larger and more comprehensive Centre of Excellence. The then BCCI secretary and current ICC chairman, Jay Shah, deserves tremendous credit for having the vision to invest in this facility and create an ecosystem of this scale. I am also grateful to the leadership for giving me the freedom and trust to develop and execute the vision we had for the CoE.

What, according to you, has been the biggest change?

For me, the biggest change is not just the infrastructure but also the ecosystem we have built around it, bringing together coaching, sports science, technology and education.

While contracted players benefit from the facility, how has it been working with domestic players, giving them more access to technology, quality coaching, and support staff?

This is extremely important to the BCCI. The CoE cannot be only for contracted players. If we want to strengthen Indian cricket, we have to strengthen the pathway beneath the international level as well. We are therefore trying to give domestic and pathway players greater access to quality coaching, sports science, performance analysis and technology. The idea is to identify potential early and give players the right environment to develop. Ultimately, CoE should contribute to the entire Indian cricket ecosystem, not just one particular group of players.

Active players have now started taking a keen interest in coaching and are going through the coaching courses. What do you attribute this trend to?

It is a very encouraging trend. Players who have played at the first-class or international level have enormous knowledge and experience, and naturally many of them want to give something back to the game. But playing and coaching are two different skill sets. That is why coach education is important. We help them understand communication, planning, leadership and most importantly, how to transfer their experience to another player. More players are now recognising that their impact on the game can continue well beyond their playing careers.

Are there any sessions for them to mentally transition from players to coaches?

It's not one session; it's an ongoing mentoring process. Transition from player to coach doesn't happen overnight. It is really a change in mindset. As a player, your primary responsibility is your own performance. As a coach, your responsibility is to make other people better. Through our coaching courses, we expose former and current players to communication, leadership, planning, managing different personalities and understanding individual players. The biggest learning is that coaching is not about showing people how much you know, but it is about helping the player discover how much they can achieve.

Can you put down in numbers the high performance camps that CoE conducts across the country in a year?

The scale of our high performance work has grown significantly. Throughout the year, we run programmes across the pathway for both men and women players from the U-16, U-19, and U-23 age groups, as well as targeted specialist skill camps, including fast and spin bowler camps. We now directly support more than 150 players annually, and the impact is clear in the outcomes we are seeing: improved skill levels, stronger readiness for international cricket, and more players progressing successfully through the pathway into higher levels. Our objective is to create a continuous pathway from age group cricket right through to international level.

The setting up of the women's coaching system -- what's that process been like?

It has been a very exciting process because women's cricket in India has grown tremendously. The support ecosystem has to grow at the same pace. We are working on a more structured system around women's cricket. We are also investing in developing coaches and support staff. Importantly, we don't want to copy the men's system. Women's cricket has its own requirements, and we need to develop expertise around those specific needs.

How much have you enjoyed watching youngsters bloom from CoE, especially the U-19 players with whom you spend a considerable amount of time?

That is one of the most rewarding parts of my role. When you see a young player come into the CoE with potential and then watch him develop not just as a cricketer but also as a person, it gives you enormous satisfaction. With U-19 players, you are dealing with an important stage of their development. You are not just preparing them for the next tournament; you are trying to give them the habits, discipline, resilience, and awareness for a long career. When you subsequently see them progress into India A or senior cricket, it is incredibly satisfying.

For somebody who's in a mentorship role, since you've travelled so much with the under-19s and the A-teams, what is that one thing that you tell them?

So with the under-19s or the A-teams, it's about getting better every day as a player in every aspect of their game. So it's not only about skill, but the mental aspect, the physical aspect, and how they can improve, because at the end of the day, any sport you play, any match you play, if you don't have that competitive spirit, then you're not a sports person. So you go out there to perform, you go out there to win the match and win the series, but at the same time, whether it's with under-19s or with the India players, it's also about measuring objectively how you're progressing after every match. It's satisfying when you see that progress in a player because the whole endeavour is: Can they reach a stage where they can win matches for the senior Indian team in any international fixture and also perform at the highest level?

There has been a lot of focus on camps in the North East; can you elaborate?

The domestic circuit and structure is so robust, and there are so many matches happening across the different age groups. There's a lot of emphasis on developing the talent in the North-East. So we have camps which are dedicated to the North-East players, men and women from U-19 to senior age group. It's great to see that every year the quality of those players has definitely gotten better, and the only way it will get better is if they get more exposure.

By playing against good teams. You test yourself and gain confidence only when you play against good teams and do well; that's how they get exposure.

How has the introduction of the U-15 category for women helped in identifying players?

We started it three years ago. It allows us to strengthen the bench and see players develop. We have players from the first batch who went on to play for India. G Kamalini was in the first batch of the U-15 tournament, and she played for India. So it's great to see not only the boys, but also the girls, benefiting from the various tournaments and camps we run under the BCCI umbrella.

When you switch roles from administrator to mentor coach, does it help that you see these players up close as an administrator?

Coaching and mentoring come naturally because, as an India player, my interactions with the youngsters were always very seamless and holistic. You share your experiences, help them evolve and develop as cricketers, and maximise their potential. The administration part is obviously a different experience, and luckily again, the structures in the BCCI system made that seamless as well. The best part of this role is getting to see so many players come, perform, get selected, attend the camps, and repeat the process the next year. So it's great to see some of the players who were attending the U-19 camps in 2022 playing for India in 2025-26.

When you look back at the almost five years of your journey at NCA/CoE, what's the most satisfying aspect?

The most satisfying thing has been seeing the ecosystem come together. It is not about one facility or one individual. It is about coaches, SSM professionals, performance analysts, grounds staff, administrators and players all working towards the same objective. I am particularly proud that the CoE has evolved into a place where players don't come only when they are injured. They come to develop their skills, improve physically, learn and become better cricketers. The most fulfilling part of this journey as the CoE head of cricket has been seeing the players' transformation, and we hope they've now achieved their dream and will continue to bring laurels to the country. Ultimately, the real success will be when these systems continue to benefit Indian cricket for many years to come.
